assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a whole class of quantum matter: a bulk insulator with protected conducting boundary states, predicted theoretically and then found in nature. The discovery is clear, original and has changed how materials are classified. It is what I look for most, a prediction that nature then confirmed, first in HgTe quantum wells and then in three-dimensional bulk crystals.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) supplied the decisive theory of the quantum spin Hall and Z2 invariant; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental realisation in HgTe; Hasan led the first three-dimensional ARPES demonstration. Mele is a close co-author of Kane and the omission is uncomfortable; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (not in the credited list) also matter for the HgTe proposal. I choose Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as a balanced theory, 2D experiment, 3D experiment trio.
assessment.maturity: Strongly mature: nearly two decades of independent confirmation across many groups and materials, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether Mele and the HgTe theory proposers should displace one of the proposed names is a genuine allocation problem.
The duplicate entry B025 bundles the quantum anomalous Hall effect; I treat that as a related but separable discovery.
Credit for the 3D experimental discovery between Hasan and other groups is not something I have independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned quantum foundations into a technology whose security rests on the laws of nature, and it links to questions about information and reality that interest me. It is original and conceptually clear, with working fibre and satellite implementations.
assessment.attribution: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard) and the entanglement-based protocol (Ekert) are the conceptual foundations. Jian-Wei Pan led the satellite and network demonstrations but I leave him out to stay within three names, and that omission is a real tension because the global network is part of the candidate title.
assessment.maturity: Foundational protocols are decades old and well tested; practical deployment and security against real-device attacks are still developing. The 2022 prize on entanglement overlaps in spirit but not in subject.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for entanglement experiments may weigh against it.
Whether this is judged physics rather than engineering and information science.
Practical security of real systems is not fully settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable, clean two-dimensional platform and created the field of moire quantum materials. It is a theory-predicted effect that an experiment found, which I value.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the flat-band prediction at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated and superconducting states. This forms a clean theory plus experiment trio from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Very reproducible and widely replicated since 2018, yet the nature of the superconductivity is still debated, so the interpretation is not fully stable and the recognition may be a little early.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.
Other early contributors (for example Cao and Fatemi, or Dean and colleagues on hBN-moire devices) are not in the credited list.
It may be judged premature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Imaging the shadow of a black hole is a discovery with an existential dimension: direct visual evidence on the strong-field regime of gravity. It is clear to the public and scientifically significant, though the black-hole existence and gravitational-wave questions were already recognised by earlier prizes.
assessment.attribution: Doeleman led the EHT collaboration and the VLBI technique; Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept; Moran contributed decades of mm-VLBI development. Credit within a collaboration of hundreds is hard to allocate fairly.
assessment.maturity: Two sources (M87* and Sgr A*) have been imaged, with polarisation results; independent reanalyses exist but tests of general relativity from the images are still limited.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit is difficult to assign to three people.
The 2020 prize already covered black holes, which may reduce appetite.
Image reconstruction depends on modelling choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos opened a new window on the cosmos, with the evidence for a blazar source and the Galactic plane. It is a genuine clue from nature, which fits my preference for observation.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube; Karle is credited as a senior leader of the construction and analysis. A two-person prize is possible. Other IceCube leaders and the earlier AMANDA contributors are outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux is firmly established (2013) and source identification keeps improving, but the origin of most events is not settled and the field is still maturing.
uncertainties: Source identification is incomplete.
Large-collaboration credit and the roles of Karle versus other leaders are uncertain.
Timing may be a few years early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays is a new observation of the universe and directly tied to cosmology and black-hole physics, with a link to my interest in what the sky tells us.
assessment.attribution: Pulsar timing array work comes from several collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA). The credited names represent leaders of different arrays, which mirrors a fair multi-array award but the proposed three are a compromise.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 evidence is about 3 to 4 sigma for the Hellings-Downs correlation, the source (supermassive binaries versus new physics) is undecided, so this is premature for now.
uncertainties: Statistical significance is below the discovery threshold in most analyses.
Origin of the signal is unresolved.
Credit across four collaborations is hard to split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic redshift at millimetre scales. It is a robust, instrument-defining discovery with a real link to gravity.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Ye's group developed the strontium clock to the highest precision. Both names are clearly supportable as a two-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with a world-wide network and redefinition of the second under discussion. The 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured optical combs and trapped ions, so overlap may argue against it.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier metrology prizes.
Other ion clock and comb contributors are outside the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-model physics, the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and other many-body problems in controllable form. It is original and broadly influential.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Cirac (with Jaksch) proposed the Hubbard simulation; Bloch's group led the experimental programme; Greiner is a strong experimental alternative. Zoller and Cirac also appear in other ballot entries, so the same names recur across candidates.
assessment.maturity: Mature for the basic Mott transition, but the claim of solving problems beyond classical reach is still in progress.
uncertainties: Overlap in names with several other quantum information candidates.
Whether the discovery is the proposal or the implementation.
Greiner and Jaksch placement is uncertain.
